07.01.title: Particle kinematics
07.01.html:
Dynamics starts with describing motion before asking what causes it. A car on a roundabout, a cyclist braking into a bend and a phone logging GPS points are all “particles”: objects whose size doesn’t matter for the question. Kinematics gives their velocity and acceleration, and the right choice of coordinates makes the physics obvious.

Cartesian coordinates

Position r(t)=(x,y). Velocity and acceleration are time derivatives:

v=r˙,a=v˙=r¨.

Simple, but it hides what a driver feels: braking versus turning.

Path coordinates

Use a unit tangent et​ along the path and a unit normal en​ towards the centre of curvature. With speed v and local radius of curvature ρ:

v=vet​,a=v˙et​+ρv2​en​.

The tangential part at​=v˙ changes the speed. The normal part an​=v2/ρ changes the direction. On a straight, ρ→∞ and an​=0. At steady speed round a circle, at​=0 but an​=v2/R still points inward.

Polar coordinates

For things that swing or spin (a radar tracking a plane, a bead sliding on a rotating rod), use r and θ:

ar​=r¨−rθ˙2,aθ​=rθ¨+2r˙θ˙.

The −rθ˙2 term is the centripetal part; 2r˙θ˙ is the Coriolis part (more in 07.12).

From measured data

A GPS log gives positions at discrete times. Differentiating once gives velocity, twice gives acceleration. Central differences work, but every differentiation amplifies measurement noise. Smoothing first trades noise for a little lag.

Worked exampleA roundabout and a GPS track

  1. A car circles a 50 m roundabout at 10 m/s, logged at 10 Hz. Central differences give at​=5×10−14, an​=1.9997 m/s² against v2/R=2, and a radius of 50.000 m.
  2. A cyclist brakes at 0.3 m/s² from 12 m/s through a 30 m bend, logged once a second. Mid-bend at 12 s: speed 8.29 m/s (true 8.40), at​=−0.27 (true −0.30), an​=2.29 m/s² (true 2.35). One-second sampling cuts corners.
  3. Add 0.5 m of GPS noise and the tangential acceleration even comes out with the wrong sign (+0.56). Accelerations from raw GPS need filtering.
  4. Polar check: r=2+0.5t, θ=0.8t at t=1.3 s gives ar​=−1.696 and aθ​=0.800 m/s², by formula and by numerical differentiation.

Exercise 1A motorway exit

A car leaves a motorway at 100 km/h on an exit ramp with a 120 m radius and brakes at 2 m/s². What is its total acceleration as it enters the curve? How fast could it go round the curve if the tyres can deliver 0.6 g in total and it stops braking?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=27.78 m/s, so an​=27.782/120=6.43 m/s².
  2. Total: 6.432+22​=6.73 m/s², about 0.69 g. Too much for 0.6 g of grip: the driver should have braked before the curve.
  3. Without braking: v2/120=0.6⋅9.81 gives v=26.6 m/s =95.7 km/h.

quiz.q: Normal acceleration (m/s²) at 10 m/s on a 50 m radius.
quiz.explain: v2/ρ.

quiz.q: Total acceleration (m/s²) of the car entering the 120 m ramp at 100 km/h while braking at 2 m/s². 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: Combine at​ and an​.

quiz.q: Highest speed (km/h) round a 120 m curve with 0.6 g of grip. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: v=aρ​.

quiz.q: At constant speed on a curve, the acceleration is…
quiz.explain: Only the normal part remains.

quiz.q: Why are accelerations from raw GPS positions so noisy?
quiz.explain: Each derivative divides noise by a small time step.
options: Differentiating twice amplifies the measurement noise

07.02.title: Newton's second law
07.02.html:
Kinematics describes motion; Newton’s second law explains it. The method is the same one used in statics (Phase 05): cut the body free, draw every force acting on it, and add them up. The only difference is that the sum is no longer zero. It equals mass times acceleration.

The law

For a particle of constant mass m:

∑F=ma.

It holds in an inertial frame, one that isn’t accelerating or rotating (the ground is close enough for most engineering). Written in components it gives one equation per direction, the same as equilibrium equations but with max​, may​ on the right.

The recipe

  1. Choose the body and draw its free-body diagram: gravity, contact forces, friction, drag, thrust.
  2. Choose coordinates (Cartesian, path or polar: whichever makes the acceleration simple).
  3. Write ∑F=ma in each direction.
  4. Solve: either algebraically, or, if forces depend on velocity or position, as a differential equation integrated in time.

Drag

Air drag on a fast body grows with the square of speed and points against the velocity:

FD​=−21​ρCD​A∣v∣v.

Now the equations couple x and y and have no simple closed-form solution. Integrate them numerically, with the RK4 method from Phase 04.

A ski jumper

Cut the jumper free in flight: gravity mg down and drag against the velocity (real jumpers also generate lift, which we leave out). Without drag, the path is the parabola of Phase 02. With drag, the jumper lands sooner and slower. The parabola is a test case: the simulation with CD​A=0 must reproduce it exactly.

Worked exampleDrag and the ski jumper

m=65 kg, v0​=25 m/s, take-off 11° down, air density 1.2 kg/m³, landing slope 35°.

  1. With zero drag, RK4 with a 1 ms step matches the parabola y=vy0​t−gt2/2 to 2.5×10−12 m.
  2. Hand check for no drag: the jumper hits the slope when vy0​t−gt2/2=−tan35°⋅vx0​t, giving t=2.531 s and 75.82 m along the slope, exactly what the simulation finds.
  3. With drag: CD​A=0.3 m² lands at 67.49 m (118 km/h), 0.5 m² at 63.07 m (108 km/h), 0.8 m² at 57.62 m (97 km/h).
  4. A tighter tuck pays off. Jumpers flying well beyond 100 m on big hills do it with lift from their V-style skis.

Exercise 1A lift in a tall building

A person of 75 kg stands on a scale in a lift. What does the scale read (in newtons and in “kg”) when the lift (a) accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s², (b) moves at constant speed, (c) slows down while going up at 2 m/s²?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Free body: weight mg down, scale force N up. N−mg=ma, so N=m(g+a) with a up positive.
  2. (a) 75⋅(9.81+1.5)=848 N, reads 86.5 kg.
  3. (b) a=0: N=736 N, reads 75 kg.
  4. (c) a=−2: N=75⋅7.81=586 N, reads 59.7 kg.

quiz.q: Scale reading (N) for 75 kg in a lift accelerating upward at 1.5 m/s². 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: N=m(g+a).

quiz.q: No-drag flight time (s) of the ski jumper before landing. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: Intersect the parabola with the slope.

quiz.q: Drag force (N) on a jumper with CD​A=0.5 m² at 25 m/s in air of 1.2 kg/m³.
quiz.explain: 21​ρCD​Av2.

quiz.q: Newton’s second law in the form ∑F=ma holds in…
quiz.explain: Non-inertial frames need extra terms (07.12).

quiz.q: Why does quadratic drag make the equations hard to solve by hand?
quiz.explain: ∣v∣ links the components.
options: It is nonlinear and couples the x and y motions

07.03.title: Work and energy
07.03.html:
Newton’s law gives the acceleration at every instant. Often you only want to know how fast something is going at a certain place: a roller coaster at the bottom of a drop, a car after braking over 30 m, a hammer as it hits a nail. Integrating F=ma along the path once and for all gives a shortcut that skips time entirely: work and energy.

The work–energy theorem

Dot mv˙=F with vdt=dr and integrate along the path from 1 to 2:

21​mv22​−21​mv12​=∫12​F⋅dr=W12​.

The change in kinetic energy equals the work done by all forces. Forces perpendicular to the motion (the normal force from a track, the tension in a pendulum string) do no work.

Conservative forces and potential energy

Some forces do work that depends only on the start and end points, not the path: gravity, springs. Their work can be stored as potential energy, Vg​=mgh and Vs​=21​kx2. If only conservative forces do work:

T+V=constant.

Friction and drag are not conservative. They take energy out, usually as heat: T2​+V2​=T1​+V1​−Wloss​.

Roller coasters

A frictionless car released at height h0​ with speed v0​ has, at height h,

v=v02​+2g(h0​−h)​.

Mass cancels and the shape of the track between doesn’t matter. The car can never climb above h0​+v02​/2g. A test: simulate the motion along the track with s¨=−gsinθ and the speeds must agree with energy everywhere.

Worked exampleThe coaster, two ways

Track profile: from 40 m down towards 10 m, a 12 m bump near x=80 m, a 17 m hill near x=150 m; 1 m/s at the top.

  1. RK4 on the path equation with a 1 ms step, 14,458 steps: largest difference from the energy speed 1.5×10−9 m/s.
  2. Speeds: 16.79 m/s at x=30 m (25 m high), 23.82 m/s = 85.8 km/h at the dip (h=10.44 m), 15.57 m/s over the last crest (h=27 m).
  3. Add rolling friction μ=0.015 and the car reaches the last crest at 14.09 m/s instead: the friction work has eaten into its energy.

Exercise 1A car brakes to a stop

A 1400 kg car brakes from 90 km/h on a level road with a constant friction force of 0.8 times its weight. How far does it travel? Then on a 10 % downhill grade?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Level: 21​mv2=μmgd, so d=v2/(2μg)=252/(2⋅0.8⋅9.81)=39.8 m. Mass cancels.
  2. Downhill, slope angle θ=arctan0.1=5.71°: gravity does positive work mgsinθd, friction μmgcosθd.
  3. d=v2/(2g(μcosθ−sinθ))=625/(2⋅9.81⋅(0.796−0.0995))=45.7 m.

quiz.q: Speed (m/s) of a frictionless coaster 30 m below its start, starting from rest. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: 2gh​.

quiz.q: Braking distance (m) from 90 km/h with friction 0.8 g on level ground. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: v2/(2μg).

quiz.q: Braking distance (m) on a 10 % downhill grade. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Gravity helps the car along.

quiz.q: The normal force from a roller-coaster track does…
quiz.explain: F⋅dr=0.
options: Positive work on the way down
Negative work on the way up
No work, being perpendicular to the motion
Work equal to mgh

quiz.q: Which of these is not a conservative force?
quiz.explain: Friction’s work depends on the path.

07.04.title: Impulse and momentum
07.04.html:
A collision lasts milliseconds and the forces during it are huge and hard to measure. Yet what happens afterwards is easy to predict, because Newton’s law integrated over time says the total momentum can’t change. Car crash reconstruction, billiards, railway couplings and a hammer driving a nail all use this.

Impulse

Integrate F=mv˙ over a time interval:

∫t1​t2​​Fdt=mv2​−mv1​.

The left side is the impulse: force times time. A small force for a long time does the same as a big force for a short time. That is why airbags and crumple zones save lives: they stretch the stopping time, so the force on the body drops.

Conservation of momentum

When two bodies collide, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite (Newton’s third law), so their impulses cancel. Without outside forces:

m1​v1​+m2​v2​=m1​v1′​+m2​v2′​.

Restitution

Momentum alone gives one equation for two unknowns. The second comes from how bouncy the impact is, described by the coefficient of restitution e:

v2′​−v1′​=−e(v2​−v1​).

e=1 is perfectly elastic (no energy lost), e=0 is perfectly plastic (the bodies stick together). Real values: steel balls about 0.9, a tennis ball 0.75, a car crash near 0.1. The kinetic energy lost is

ΔT=21​(1−e2)m1​+m2​m1​m2​​(v1​−v2​)2.

Worked exampleTwo lab carts

Cart 1, 0.5 kg at 2 m/s, hits cart 2, 1.0 kg at rest.

  1. e=1: v1′​=−0.667 m/s (bounces back), v2′​=1.333 m/s, no energy lost.
  2. e=0.6: v1′​=−0.133, v2′​=1.067 m/s; 0.427 J lost, matching 21​(1−0.36)⋅31​⋅4.
  3. e=0: both move off at 0.667 m/s; 0.667 J lost, two thirds of the original energy.
  4. Momentum before and after agrees to machine precision in 10,000 random collisions (worst relative error 5×10−16).
  5. A ball with e=0.8 dropped from 1 m bounces to 0.64, 0.41, 0.26 m: each height is e2 times the last.

Exercise 1A railway shunting impact

A 30 t wagon rolling at 1.5 m/s hits a stationary 20 t wagon and they couple (e=0). Find the common speed, the energy absorbed by the buffers and coupling, and the average force if the impact lasts 0.4 s.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Common speed: 30⋅1.5/(30+20)=0.9 m/s.
  2. Energy lost: 21​⋅5030⋅20​⋅103⋅1.52=13.5 kJ.
  3. Impulse on the second wagon: 20000⋅0.9=18,000 N s, so the average force is 18000/0.4=45 kN.

quiz.q: Common speed (m/s) after the 30 t and 20 t wagons couple.
quiz.explain: Momentum.

quiz.q: Energy absorbed (kJ) in that coupling.
quiz.explain: 21​μv2 with e=0.

quiz.q: Rebound speed (m/s) of cart 1 (0.5 kg, 2 m/s) hitting 1.0 kg at rest with e=0.6, with sign. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Momentum plus restitution.

quiz.q: Airbags reduce injuries because they…
quiz.explain: Same impulse, longer time.
options: Increase the stopping time, lowering the force

quiz.q: In a collision with e=1 between equal masses, one at rest…
quiz.explain: Newton’s cradle.
options: The moving one bounces back at full speed

07.05.title: The rocket equation
07.05.html:
A rocket pushes itself forward by throwing mass backward. As it burns fuel it gets lighter, so the same thrust accelerates it harder. Newton’s law in its plain form assumes constant mass, so rockets need a careful derivation, and the result explains why rockets are mostly fuel and why they have stages.

Momentum over a short time

At time t the rocket has mass m and speed v. In dt it ejects mass dme​ backwards at speed ve​ relative to itself. With no outside forces, total momentum stays the same:

mv=(m−dme​)(v+dv)+dme​(v−ve​).

Expanding and dropping the tiny product dme​dv gives mdv=ve​dme​. The thrust is ve​m˙e​. Since dme​=−dm:

dv=−ve​mdm​⇒Δv=ve​lnm1​m0​​.

This is Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation. The speed gained depends only on the exhaust speed and the mass ratio, not on how fast the fuel burns.

Gravity

Flying straight up with gravity, mv˙=m˙e​ve​−mg. Integrating over the burn time tb​ gives Δv=ve​ln(m0​/m1​)−gtb​. The gravity loss gtb​ is why rockets burn hard and fast at lift-off.

Why stages

The logarithm is cruel. Reaching low Earth orbit needs about 9.3 km/s including gravity and drag losses. With a good kerosene engine, ve​≈3 km/s, so m0​/m1​=e3.1≈22: 95 % of the rocket must be propellant. Dropping empty tanks and engines along the way (staging) means the later stages don’t have to accelerate dead weight.

Worked exampleA sounding rocket

Lift-off mass 1000 kg, 750 kg of propellant, ve​=2500 m/s, burning 15 kg/s for 50 s.

  1. Tsiolkovsky: Δv=2500ln(1000/250)=3465.736 m/s. RK4 on mv˙=m˙ve​ gives the same to 10−6 m/s.
  2. With gravity: burnout at 54.98 km and 2975.2 m/s. The difference is exactly gtb​=490.5 m/s.
  3. Thrust is 37.5 kN, a thrust-to-weight ratio of 3.82 at lift-off.
  4. Staging: drop a 60 kg tank after 500 kg of propellant and the same rocket reaches 3832 m/s instead of 3466 m/s.
  5. Coasting without drag would carry it to 506 km. Real sounding rockets of this size reach far less, because of air drag and the fact that real ones carry payloads.

Exercise 1How much propellant?

A spacecraft of 2000 kg (dry) needs a Δv of 1500 m/s for an orbit change. Its engine has ve​=3100 m/s. How much propellant must it carry?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. m0​/m1​=e1500/3100=e0.4839=1.6224.
  2. m0​=1.6224⋅2000=3245 kg, so it needs 1245 kg of propellant: 38 % of the fuelled mass.

quiz.q: Δv (m/s) for ve​=2500 m/s and mass ratio 4. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: ve​ln(m0​/m1​).

quiz.q: Propellant (kg) for 1500 m/s on a 2000 kg dry spacecraft with ve​=3100 m/s. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: m1​(eΔv/ve​−1).

quiz.q: Gravity loss (m/s) for a 50 s vertical burn.
quiz.explain: gtb​.

quiz.q: Doubling the mass ratio of a rocket adds to its Δv…
quiz.explain: Logarithm.
options: Double the Δv
A fixed ve​ln2
Four times the Δv

quiz.q: Rockets use stages mainly to…
quiz.explain: Dead weight hurts the mass ratio.
options: Stop accelerating empty tanks and engines

07.06.title: Systems of particles
07.06.html:
A car is thousands of parts, a rocket sheds exhaust, a gymnast moves her arms in mid-air. Treating each as one particle seems too crude. Yet one result makes it legitimate for the overall motion: the centre of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted on it.

The centre of mass theorem

For particles i with masses mi​ at positions ri​, define the total mass M and the centre of mass

rG​=M1​i∑​mi​ri​.

Write Newton’s law for each particle, splitting forces into external Fi​ and internal fij​ (from particle j on i):

mi​r¨i​=Fi​+j=i∑​fij​.

Add all of them. By Newton’s third law fij​=−fji​, so the internal forces cancel in pairs:

Mr¨G​=i∑​Fi​.

Consequences

  • With no external force, the centre of mass moves in a straight line at constant speed, and total momentum Mr˙G​ is conserved. That’s what made the collision problems of 07.04 solvable.
  • A diver can’t change the path of her centre of mass in the air: it follows a parabola whatever she does with her body.
  • An exploding firework’s fragments scatter, but their centre of mass continues along the original parabola (until fragments hit the ground).

N-body simulation

A good test of any simulation of interacting particles: the internal forces must sum to zero at every step, and momentum must stay constant to rounding error. The velocity Verlet method, used for molecular dynamics and planetary motion, keeps this property exactly.

Worked exampleFive bodies

Five masses between 0.5 and 2.0 (total 5.200) with random positions and velocities, attracting each other.

  1. Initial momentum (0.302751, 0.538379), so the centre of mass moves at (0.0582, 0.1035).
  2. After 5000 velocity-Verlet steps the momentum is unchanged to 6 decimals and beyond, and the centre of mass is within 3×10−14 of the straight line.
  3. The sum of mi​ai​ at the start is (−2×10−15,−1×10−15): zero up to rounding.
  4. With a uniform external gravity of 1 downward, the centre of mass lands at (−0.059615,−11.959423) after 5 time units, exactly the single-particle prediction r0​+vG​t+21​gt2.

Exercise 1A boat and a walker

A 70 kg person walks 4 m from the stern to the bow of a 210 kg boat floating at rest. Ignoring water resistance, how far does the boat move?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. No horizontal external force, and everything starts at rest: the centre of mass stays put.
  2. If the boat moves x backwards, the person moves 4−x forwards relative to the water: 70(4−x)=210x.
  3. x=280/280=1.0 m. The person moves 3.0 m relative to the water.

quiz.q: Distance (m) the 210 kg boat moves when a 70 kg person walks 4 m along it.
quiz.explain: The centre of mass stays put.

quiz.q: Centre of mass position (m) of 2 kg at x=0 and 3 kg at x=5.
quiz.explain: ∑mi​xi​/M.

quiz.q: A 4 kg firework at 30 m/s explodes into 1 kg and 3 kg pieces. The 1 kg piece moves at 60 m/s in the original direction. Speed (m/s) of the 3 kg piece.
quiz.explain: Momentum is conserved.

quiz.q: Why do internal forces drop out of the centre of mass equation?
quiz.explain: fij​=−fji​.
options: They cancel in pairs by Newton’s third law

quiz.q: A diver tucks during a dive. Her centre of mass…
quiz.explain: Only gravity acts externally.

07.07.title: Angular momentum of particles
07.07.html:
A figure skater pulls in her arms and spins faster. A satellite moves fastest when closest to Earth. A ball on a string wound around a pole speeds up as the string shortens. All three follow from one law: the rate of change of angular momentum equals the applied moment, and if the moment is zero, angular momentum is conserved.

Angular momentum

For a particle of mass m at position r (from a fixed point O) with velocity v:

LO​=r×mv.

In the plane, with polar coordinates, L=mr2θ˙: only the transverse velocity rθ˙ counts.

The law

Differentiate: L˙O​=r˙×mv+r×mv˙. The first term is zero (a vector crossed with itself), and mv˙=F, so

L˙O​=r×F=MO​.

A central force, always pointing towards or away from O (string tension, gravity from a planet), has no moment about O. Then mr2θ˙ is constant.

The shrinking string

A mass whirls on a string pulled in through a hole. The string pulls radially, so L is conserved and

ω=ω0​(rr0​​)2.

Halve the radius and the spin rate quadruples. Kinetic energy is not conserved: it grows as 1/r2, and the extra energy comes from the work done pulling the string against the growing tension mrω2.

Worked examplePulling in the string

m=0.2 kg, r0​=0.8 m, ω0​=2π rad/s. The string is pulled in at 0.15 m/s for 4 s, to 0.2 m.

  1. RK4 on the transverse polar equation rθ¨+2r˙θ˙=0: ω rises to 100.531 rad/s (16 rev/s), as predicted by ω0​(r0​/r)2=16ω0​.
  2. L=0.804248 kg m²/s before and after, a relative change of 2×10−12.
  3. Kinetic energy rises from 2.527 J to 40.426 J. The difference, 37.899 J, equals ∫mrω2dr, the work done on the string.
  4. The tension climbs from 6.32 N to 404 N. Pulling in a fast-spinning mass gets very hard.

Exercise 1A satellite’s speed

A satellite in an elliptical orbit is 7000 km from Earth’s centre at perigee, moving at 8.0 km/s perpendicular to the radius. At apogee it is 10,500 km away. How fast is it moving there?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Gravity is central, so L=mrv⊥​ is conserved. At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the radius.
  2. va​=vp​rp​/ra​=8.0⋅7000/10500=5.33 km/s.

quiz.q: Spin rate (rad/s) when the string is pulled from 0.8 m to 0.4 m, starting at 2π rad/s. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: ω0​(r0​/r)2.

quiz.q: Satellite speed (km/s) at apogee, 10,500 km, if it is 8.0 km/s at perigee, 7000 km. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: rp​vp​=ra​va​.

quiz.q: Angular momentum (kg m²/s) of 0.2 kg at 0.8 m spinning at 2π rad/s. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: mr2ω.

quiz.q: Angular momentum about O is conserved when…
quiz.explain: Central force, zero moment.
options: The force always passes through O

quiz.q: When the string is pulled in, the kinetic energy…
quiz.explain: T=L2/(2mr2) grows.
options: Increases, from the work done pulling

07.08.title: Rigid body kinematics in 2D
07.08.html:
Windscreen wipers, bicycle suspensions, excavator arms, sewing machines and the pedals of a cross-trainer are linkages: rigid links joined by pins. Designing them means knowing where every point goes and how fast, for every input angle. One equation, applied link by link, does it.

Velocity of two points on one body

A rigid body moving in the plane has one angular velocity ω (the same for every line drawn on it). For two points A and B on it:

vB​=vA​+ω×rAB​.

The relative velocity ω×rAB​ is perpendicular to AB with size ω∣AB∣. Differentiating again:

aB​=aA​+α×rAB​−ω2rAB​.

The last term is the centripetal part, pointing from B back towards A.

The four-bar linkage

Four links in a loop: ground d, crank a, coupler b, rocker c. Given the crank angle:

  1. Position: joint A is on the crank circle; joint B is where the circle of radius b about A meets the circle of radius c about the rocker pivot.
  2. Velocity: write vB​ twice, once through the coupler (vA​+ω3​×rAB​) and once through the rocker (ω4​×rO4​B​). Equating them gives two equations for ω3​ and ω4​.

Grashof’s rule

Will the crank turn all the way round, or jam? Sort the link lengths: shortest s, longest l, the others p, q. If

s+l≤p+q,

the linkage is Grashof and at least one link can turn fully relative to the others. With the shortest link as the crank, the crank turns fully and the rocker swings back and forth: a crank-rocker. If s+l>p+q, no link can make a full turn.

Worked exampleA wiper-style linkage

a=20, b=70, c=45, d=70 mm. Sorted: 20 + 70 = 90 ≤ 45 + 70 = 115: Grashof, with the crank shortest.

  1. At 60° and 1 rev/s: A = (10, 17.321), B = (74.387, 44.786).
  2. Solving the velocity equations: ω3​=−0.8456, ω4​=1.9114 rad/s; ∣vA​∣=125.66 mm/s, ∣vB​∣=86.01 mm/s.
  3. Differentiating the rocker angle numerically gives the same ω4​ to 10−5.
  4. Over one crank turn the rocker swings 55.4°, between 79.3° and 134.6°.
  5. In 400 random linkages with the shortest link as the crank, Grashof’s rule predicted full rotation correctly every time.

Exercise 1Which linkage turns?

For each set (crank listed first, then coupler, rocker, ground, in mm), say whether the crank can turn fully: (a) 30, 80, 60, 70; (b) 40, 50, 60, 90; (c) 50, 30, 60, 70.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. (a) s+l=30+80=110≤60+70=130, Grashof, crank is shortest: turns fully.
  2. (b) 40+90=130>50+60=110: non-Grashof, nothing turns fully.
  3. (c) 30+70=100≤50+60=110: Grashof, but the shortest link is the coupler, not the crank. The coupler can turn fully relative to the others, but the crank only rocks: a double-rocker.

07.09.title: Planar rigid body dynamics
07.09.html:
Roll a solid disc and a hoop of the same mass and radius down a ramp, and the disc wins every time. Mass and radius don’t matter at all. What matters is how the mass is spread around the axis. Explaining this needs Newton’s law for rotation as well as translation.

Equations of motion in the plane

A rigid body in plane motion has three degrees of freedom: two for the centre of mass G and one for rotation. Three equations:

∑Fx​=maGx​,∑Fy​=maGy​,∑MG​=IG​α.

IG​ is the moment of inertia about G (next lesson). Moments must be taken about G, or about a fixed point, or else extra terms appear.

Rolling without slipping

A wheel of radius r rolling without slipping has its contact point momentarily at rest, so vG​=ωr and aG​=αr. That is the rolling constraint. Friction at the contact supplies the moment that spins the wheel up, and does no work, since the contact point doesn’t move.

Down a ramp

Write IG​=kmr2. Along the ramp: ma=mgsinθ−F. About G: Fr=IG​α=kmr2⋅a/r. Eliminate F:

a=1+kgsinθ​,F=1+kk​mgsinθ.

Solid sphere (k=2/5): a=75​gsinθ. Solid disc (k=1/2): 32​gsinθ. Thin ring (k=1): 21​gsinθ. The bigger k, the more of the energy goes into spinning rather than moving.

To roll without slipping, the friction needed must be available: F≤μN=μmgcosθ, which gives μ≥1+kk​tanθ.

Worked exampleThe race at 10°

A 2 m ramp at 10°, gsinθ=1.7035 m/s².

  1. Sliding block (no friction): 1.7035 m/s², 1.532 s.
  2. Solving the two equations for each shape: sphere 1.2168 m/s² (1.813 s), disc 1.1357 m/s² (1.877 s), ring 0.8517 m/s² (2.167 s). The disc’s acceleration is exactly 32​gsinθ, the ring’s 21​gsinθ.
  3. Energy check for the disc: mgh=21​mv2+21​Iω2=43​mv2 gives v=4gh/3​=2.1313 m/s, the same as the simulation.
  4. Friction needed per kg: disc 0.568 N, ring 0.852 N. The disc rolls without slipping if μ≥tan10°/3=0.0588.

Exercise 1A yo-yo

A yo-yo is a solid disc of mass m and radius R with its string wound round an axle of radius r=R/4. Released from rest with the string held fixed, what is its downward acceleration and the string tension?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Down: ma=mg−T. About G: Tr=21​mR2α, with the constraint a=αr.
  2. So T=21​mR2a/r2=8ma (using R/r=4).
  3. ma=mg−8ma gives a=g/9=1.09 m/s², and T=98​mg.

07.10.title: Moment of inertia
07.10.html:
Mass tells you how hard it is to push something into motion; the moment of inertia tells you how hard it is to spin it. A flywheel stores energy by having a large one, a racing wheel accelerates quickly by having a small one, and a figure skater changes hers by moving her arms. It depends on where the mass sits, not only how much there is.

Definition

For a body rotating about an axis, each bit of mass dm at distance r from the axis contributes r2dm:

I=∫r2dm.

The radius of gyration k is defined by I=mk2: the radius at which all the mass could sit to give the same I.

Standard results

Body (axis) I
Thin ring, radius R mR2
Solid disc or cylinder 21​mR2
Thick ring, radii R1​, R2​ 21​m(R12​+R22​)
Solid sphere 52​mR2
Slender rod, about its centre 121​mL2

The parallel-axis theorem

If IG​ is about an axis through the centre of mass, then about a parallel axis a distance d away:

I=IG​+md2.

A small mass far from the axis matters far more than its own spin.

From a drawing

For a wheel symmetric about its axis with thickness t(r), a thin ring at radius r has dm=ρt(r)2πrdr, so I=∫ρt(r)2πr3dr. That one integral handles any profile. It’s what CAD mass-properties tools compute, and a check against simple shapes proves the code.

Worked exampleChecking shapes, then an engine flywheel

Steel, ρ=7850 kg/m³.

  1. Solid disc 400 × 30 mm: m=29.594 kg, I=0.591876 kg m², equal to 21​mR2.
  2. Ring from 300 to 400 mm diameter, 30 mm thick: m=12.947 kg, I=0.404603 kg m², equal to 21​m(R12​+R22​).
  3. A flywheel for a stationary engine: hub 60 mm wide from a 30 mm bore to 60 mm diameter, a 20 mm web out to 320 mm diameter, then a 60 mm rim to 400 mm. m=34.49 kg, I=0.86087 kg m², radius of gyration 158 mm.
  4. The rim is 62 % of the mass but 81 % of the inertia.
  5. A 0.5 kg balance mass bolted on at 150 mm adds 0.5⋅0.152=0.01125 kg m² by the parallel-axis term; its spin about its own axis adds only 2.5×10−5.
  6. At 3000 rpm the flywheel stores 21​Iω2=42.48 kJ.

Exercise 1A bicycle wheel

A bicycle wheel has a 0.45 kg rim and tyre at an effective radius of 0.33 m, 32 spokes of 6 g each running from the hub (radius 0.03 m) to the rim, and a 0.3 kg hub of radius 0.03 m. Estimate its moment of inertia, treating the spokes as thin rods.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Rim and tyre: 0.45⋅0.332=0.0490 kg m².
  2. Spokes: a rod from 0.03 to 0.33 m has I=3m​⋅r2​−r1​r23​−r13​​=30.006​⋅0.30.035937−0.000027​=2.394×10−4 kg m² each; 32 of them: 0.00766 kg m².
  3. Hub, as a solid cylinder: 21​⋅0.3⋅0.032=0.000135 kg m².
  4. Total about 0.0568 kg m². The rim dominates, which is why light rims matter so much to climbers.
